{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2018}}
In [[measure theory]], '''[[projection (mathematics)|projection]] maps ''' often appear when working with product (Cartesian) spaces: The [[product sigma-algebra]] of [[measurable space]]s is defined to be the finest such that the [[Projection (set theory)|projection mappings]] will be [[measurable function|measurable]]. Sometimes for some reasons product spaces are equipped with {{sigma}}-algebra different than ''the'' product {{sigma}}-algebra. In these cases the projections need not be measurable at all.

The projected set of a [[measurable set]] is called [[analytic set]] and need not be a measurable set. However, in some cases, either relatively to the product {{sigma}}-algebra or relatively to some other {{sigma}}-algebra, projected set of measurable set is indeed measurable.

[[Henri Lebesgue]] himself, one of the founders of measure theory, was mistaken about that fact. In a paper from 1905 he wrote that the projection of Borel set in the [[plane (geometry)|plane]] onto the [[real line]] is again a Borel set.<ref>Lebesgue, H. (1905) [https://eudml.org/doc/234955 Sur les fonctions représentables analytiquement]. Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées. Vol. 1, 139–216.</ref> The mathematician [[Mikhail Yakovlevich Suslin]] found that error about ten years later, and his following research has led to [[descriptive set theory]].<ref name="Moschovakis">{{cite book | author-link=Yiannis N. Moschovakis | author=Moschovakis, Yiannis N. | title=Descriptive Set Theory|url=https://www.math.ucla.edu/~ynm/books.htm | publisher=North Holland | year=1980|page=2 |isbn=0-444-70199-0}}</ref> The fundamental mistake of Lebesgue was to think that projection commutes with decreasing intersection, while there are simple counterexamples to that.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://almostsure.wordpress.com/2016/11/08/measurable-projection-and-the-debut-theorem/#more-1873 |title=Measurable Projection and the Debut Theorem |last=Lowther |first=George |date=8 November 2016 |website=Almost Sure |access-date=21 March 2018}}</ref>

==Basic examples==

For an example of a non-measurable set with measurable [[Projection (set theory)|projections]], consider the space <math>X := \{0, 1\}</math> with the {{sigma}}-algebra <math>\mathcal{F} := \{\varnothing, \{0\}, \{1\}, \{0, 1\}\}</math> and the space <math>Y := \{0, 1\}</math> with the {{sigma}}-algebra <math>\mathcal{G} := \{\varnothing, \{0, 1\}\}.</math> The diagonal set <math>\{(0, 0), (1, 1)\} \subseteq X \times Y</math> is not measurable relatively to <math>\mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{G},</math> although the both projections are measurable sets.

The common example for a non-measurable set which is a projection of a measurable set, is in [[Lebesgue sigma-algebra|Lebesgue {{sigma}}-algebra]]. Let <math>\mathcal{L}</math> be Lebesgue {{sigma}}-algebra of <math>\Reals</math> and let <math>\mathcal{L}'</math> be the Lebesgue {{sigma}}-algebra of <math>\Reals^2.</math> For any bounded <math>N \subseteq \Reals</math> not in <math>\mathcal{L}.</math> the set <math>N \times \{0\}</math> is in <math>\mathcal{L}',</math> since [[Lebesgue measure]] is [[complete measure|complete]] and the product set is contained in a set of measure zero.

Still one can see that <math>\mathcal{L}'</math> is not the product {{sigma}}-algebra <math>\mathcal{L} \otimes \mathcal{L}</math> but its completion. As for such example in product {{sigma}}-algebra, one can take the space <math>\{0, 1\}^\Reals</math> (or any product along a set with cardinality greater than continuum) with the product {{sigma}}-algebra <math>\mathcal{F} = \textstyle {\bigotimes\limits_{t\in\Reals}} \mathcal{F}_t</math> where <math>\mathcal{F}_t = \{\varnothing,\{0\} ,\{1\} ,\{0, 1\}\}</math> for every <math>t \in \Reals.</math> In fact, in this case "most" of the projected sets are not measurable, since the cardinality of <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is <math>\aleph_0 \cdot 2^{\aleph_0} = 2^{\aleph_0},</math> whereas the cardinality of the projected sets is <math>2^{2^{\aleph_0}}.</math> There are also examples of Borel sets in the plane which their projection to the real line is not a Borel set, as Suslin showed.<ref name="Moschovakis" />

==Measurable projection theorem==

The following theorem gives a sufficient condition for the projection of measurable sets to be measurable.

Let <math>(X, \mathcal{F})</math> be a measurable space and let <math>(Y, \mathcal{B})</math> be a [[polish space]] where <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is its Borel {{sigma}}-algebra. Then for every set in the product {{sigma}}-algebra <math>\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{B},</math> the projected set onto <math>X</math> is a [[universally measurable set]] relatively to <math>\mathcal{F}.</math><ref>* {{cite book|last=Crauel |first=Hans |title=Random Probability Measures on Polish Spaces |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RhT_aZGqmQEC&dq=measurable+projection+theorem&pg=PA13 |location=London |publisher=CRC Press |page=13 |isbn=0415273870 |series=STOCHASTICS MONOGRAPHS|year=2003}}</ref>

An important special case of this theorem is that the projection of any Borel set of <math>\Reals^n</math> onto <math>\Reals^{n-k}</math> where <math>k < n</math> is Lebesgue-measurable, even though it is not necessarily a Borel set. In addition, it means that the former example of non-Lebesgue-measurable set of <math>\Reals</math> which is a projection of some measurable set of <math>\Reals^2,</math> is the only sort of such example.
